 ■ Kim Ki-dong, FC Seoul manager who captured the K League 1 crown after a decade
Kept his promise to fans despite chants of "Get out"
Turned down a transfer during the dark days, even held a town-hall meeting with supporters
"I feel I have to start all over again," he says of his ambitions
Emphasizes fighting spirit and defense, builds a team culture
 Sports | Published 2026.11.15. 15:05:30 | By Lee Jong-ho phillies@sedaily.com | Summary | Save A A A FC Seoul manager Kim Ki-dong, who led the K League 1 club to its first title in 10 years, poses with a soccer ball during an interview with Seoul Economic Daily at GS Champions Park in Guri, Gyeonggi Province, on Dec. 13. Photo by Cho Tae-hyung FC Seoul manager Kim Ki-dong, who led the K League 1 club to its first title in 10 years, poses during an interview with Seoul Economic Daily at GS Champions Park in Guri, Gyeonggi Province, on Dec. 13. Photo by Cho Tae-hyung FC Seoul manager Kim Ki-dong, who led the K League 1 club to its first title in 10 years, speaks during an interview with Seoul Economic Daily at GS Champions Park in Guri, Gyeonggi Province, on Dec. 13. Photo by Cho Tae-hyung GURI — Stadiums filled with sharp jeers and chants of "Kim Ki-dong out." Five straight seasons sliding into Final B, the bottom half of the standings for teams ranked seventh through 12th. And a long, dark 10-year tunnel without a trophy. FC Seoul, one of the giants of professional soccer's K League 1, has finally returned to the throne after breaking through a mountain of doubt from the edge of a cliff.
 When he took the job in 2024, Kim Ki-dong declared he would "lift a trophy within three years without fail." He silenced every criticism with results and turned that promise into reality. Drawing on his trademark forceful leadership, he overhauled the club's makeup and restored the pride of a storied franchise in his third season at the helm. Seoul clinched the K League 1 title on Oct. 24 with five matches still left on the calendar.
 Meeting with Seoul Economic Daily on the 13th at GS Champions Park in Guri, FC Seoul's training ground, Kim was more composed than euphoric. "A lot of things crossed my mind the moment we reached the goal, but once this time passes it is just another part of the past," he said. "Seoul is a team that always has to push toward the top, so what I feel most is that we have to start again."
 The road to that glory was anything but smooth. Early in the 2024 season the team sank as low as 10th. Last year, criticism mounted over the club's parting with franchise star Ki Sung-yueng, now at Pohang. After two consecutive seasons of turmoil, fan frustration boiled over to the point where the team bus was blocked after a match. At one stage Kim even received a suggestion from an agent about moving to another club.
 Each time, he chose to face the problem head-on. He held a town hall with supporters and worked to resolve the conflict himself. To the agent who floated the transfer, he said flatly that "if I leave now, the label of a failed manager will follow me for the rest of my life." Kim looked back and said, "There was a stretch when I told my coaching staff, 'If we don't make Final A' — the top six — 'we all pack our bags.' Because we went through that, this year's glory was possible."
 Kim pointed to a four-match winning run early in the campaign as the turning point of the title season. "After the pain of losing our opening match two years in a row, when we put together four straight wins at the start, I became convinced that at this pace we could compete for the title," he said.
 Even while holding a commanding lead all season, he refused to let anyone talk prematurely about a championship. He skipped even a pop-up store event the club staged in Seongsu-dong. "With the title not yet secured, I judged that if I as the manager started smiling and enjoying myself, the squad could grow complacent, so I kept the tension up to the very end," he said.
 Behind Seoul's title was a team culture Kim rebuilt from scratch. Having diagnosed early in his tenure that "there are plenty of players who can strike a ball well, but the fighting spirit to battle as a team is lacking," he focused on instilling a one-team culture at a club where individualism had taken root.
 A clear selection policy was central to that. "The rule was that the starter is not the player I like but the player who helps the team and is in good form, and I kept that without compromise," Kim said. "Once I held firm to that rule, the players themselves created an atmosphere of fiercely managing their own condition."
 Tactically, he invested in defensive stability and balance between attack and defense. Learning from the heavy run of conceded goals that destabilized the team after Kim Ju-sung left for Sanfrecce Hiroshima last year, he rebuilt the back line around Yazan Al-Arab of Jordan and Juan Antonio Ros of Spain, and completed the team's spine by signing Hrvoje Babec of Croatia for midfield. The fact that attacking output was spread evenly among Song Min-kyu, now at CD Nacional, Jeong Seung-won and Lee Seung-mo, rather than concentrated on one player, was another product of ideal team soccer.
 The other pillar of the club's transformation was the arrival of veterans with deep title-winning experience, including Kim Jin-su, Moon Seon-min and Song Min-kyu. "When a crisis came, it was far more effective to have seniors who had won titles hold the center than for the manager to say a hundred words," Kim said.
 He was especially effusive about the leadership of captain Kim Jin-su. "Because Jin-su was there, an achievement like this title was possible," he said. "He taught the young players basic manners and discipline, and behind the scenes he bought them meals and looked after their troubles, binding the team together."
 Having won league titles and the Korea Cup, formerly the FA Cup, over the course of his managerial career, Kim now turns his gaze to Asia. "Since I began managing, I have lifted trophies in the league and the Korea Cup, but my best result on the Asian stage is a runner-up finish," he said. (He won the old FA Cup with Pohang in 2023 and finished runner-up with Pohang in 2021.) "I want to take on the AFC Champions League Elite title that everyone says is difficult and complete the run." Seoul, which had been in ACL2, enters the ACLE next year as K League 1 champion.
 Kim added that aggressive investment by the club is essential if Seoul is to become the league's true leading club rather than a one-off champion. "The reality is that when we compete for the same player against rivals like Jeonbuk Hyundai Motors, Ulsan and Daejeon, we are outgunned financially," he said. "I hope that Honorary Chairman Huh Chang-soo, Chairman Huh Tae-soo and GS Group as a whole will invest more."
